title: Probability
body:
[[Bernoulli Distribution]]

---

Probability is the model of the mechanism that produced your data. [[Descriptive Statistics]]
summarises what you got; probability describes what could have happened, so that block 3 onward can
say how surprising what you got actually was. **The inference half of [[STATISTICS]] is probability
run backwards.**

## The setup

- **Sample space** $S$: the set of every possible outcome. A coin gives $\{H, T\}$, two dice give
  36 ordered pairs, a lifetime measurement gives $[0, \infty)$.
- **Event**: any subset of $S$. "The dice sum to 7" is a set of six outcomes.
- **Probability**: a function from events to $[0,1]$.

**Events are [[Sets]], and this is not an analogy.** Union is "or", intersection is "and",
complement is "not", disjoint means mutually exclusive, and De Morgan's laws hold unchanged. Venn
diagrams are that note's material and every identity below is a set identity with $P$ applied.
[[DISCRETE MATH]] owns this and it is not restated here.

## The axioms

Three, and everything else is derived from them:

1. $P(A) \geq 0$ for every event
2. $P(S) = 1$
3. $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$ when $A$ and $B$ are disjoint

Immediate consequences:

| Result | Why |
|---|---|
| $P(\varnothing) = 0$ | complement of $S$ |
| $P(A^c) = 1 - P(A)$ | $A \cup A^c = S$ and they are disjoint |
| $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$ | inclusion-exclusion: the overlap was counted twice |
| $A \subseteq B \implies P(A) \leq P(B)$ | monotonicity |

**$P(A^c) = 1 - P(A)$ is the most useful line in the course.** "At least one" problems are almost
always easier as $1 - P(\text{none})$, because "none" is a single intersection and "at least one" is
a mess of overlapping cases.

## Counting

When outcomes are equally likely, probability collapses to counting:

$$
P(A) = \frac{|A|}{|S|}
$$

and the whole problem becomes combinatorics. [[Permutation]] when order matters, [[Combination]]
when it does not, both from [[DISCRETE MATH]] with their derivations. The two failure modes are
counting ordered outcomes in the numerator and unordered in the denominator, and forgetting that
"equally likely" was an assumption.

Worked example, the **birthday problem**, because it is the one that connects to
[[Hashing]]:

```
P(all 23 people have different birthdays)
  = (365/365)(364/365)(363/365) ... (343/365)
  ≈ 0.493

so P(at least one shared birthday) ≈ 0.507
```

Computed as $1 - P(\text{none})$, exactly as above. **23 people is enough for a better-than-even
chance of a collision**, which feels wrong and is the reason it is famous: the number of *pairs*
grows as $\binom{n}{2}$, not as $n$. That is the same argument that says a hash table starts
colliding at around $\sqrt{m}$ keys for $m$ buckets, and it is why [[Hashing]] needs collision
resolution rather than treating collisions as a rare accident.

## Conditioning

$P(A \mid B)$ is where the subject gets interesting, and it gets its own notes:
[[Conditional Probability]] for the definition, independence, and the multiplication rule, and
[[Bayes Theorem]] for inverting one.

**Mutually exclusive is not independent.** Disjoint events with non-zero probability are as
dependent as events get, since knowing $A$ occurred tells you $B$ did not. Confusing the two is the
single most common error in block 2.

## Related

- [[Random Variable]]: attaching numbers to outcomes, which is how probability becomes computable
- [[Probability Distribution]]: the standard families and which question each answers
- [[Bernoulli Distribution]]: the simplest case, one trial with two outcomes
- [[Sets]], [[Permutation]], [[Combination]] ([[DISCRETE MATH]]): the machinery this borrows
- [[Random Numbers]] and [[Simulation]] ([[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]]): estimating a probability by
  sampling when the counting argument is too hard
- [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]]: average-case analysis is an expectation over an assumed input
  distribution, and randomised algorithms make that assumption true by force
